# Harness

Four lanes, four agents, one kernel. Code decides what code can decide; the model fills the rest. `harness` below means `node .claude/bin/harness.mjs`.

## Every request

1. A change request: run `harness admit --text "<request>" --human` and invoke the one lane skill it names: `expediting` (fast), `ordering` (order), `designing` (design), `researching` (research). Never load a second lane skill to compare. A plain question: answer it.
2. State lives in `work/<id>/`. Read it with `harness state <id>` and `harness next <id>`. Never remember or re-derive it. `harness route` is the only way a verdict changes state.
3. Agents in `.claude/agents/`: analyst, architect, developer, reviewer. Spawn by role name, continue a live instance with `SendMessage`, never respawn one. The one fresh spawn: the cumulative review gets a new reviewer, `cumulative-reviewer`.
4. Stop only at a user gate. The gate packet is `harness next` rendered: one line what happened, one line what changed, the bracket options. Never two stops in a row.
5. Verdict tokens are exact and stand alone on the last line: `APPROVED`, `CHANGES REQUIRED`, `ALIGNED`, `DRIFT DETECTED`, `PHASE DONE`, `PHASE STALLED`, `ARTIFACT WRITTEN`, `REPORT WRITTEN`, `AMENDED`. A near miss is not a verdict.

## Rules

`.claude/rules/` loads by path: `work-items` (work/**), `security-paths`, `harness-authoring` (.claude/**), `prose` (always), `comments` (always).

## Project facts

Operational one-liners every agent needs and none should rediscover. Append below.

- Sources (read-only repos such as `analysis`) are declared in `.claude/harness.json`; each root comes from its env var, set in the `env` block of `.claude/settings.local.json`. Reach them with `harness source find|grep` and the work item's snapshots; nothing writes under a source.

# Comments in code Always loaded. It covers every agent and the lead, in every lane. It wins over any project rule, such as a language rule's `## Comments` section, that allows comments or doc comments. Write no new comments in code. Names, types, small functions and tests carry the meaning. If a comment seems needed to explain what code does, rename or extract instead. The ban covers every comment form, doc comments included: XML ``, ``, ``, ``, ``; JSDoc; Python docstrings; markup comments; line and block comments of any language. Only these lines are exempt: machine directives (`eslint-disable`, `@ts-expect-error`, `noqa`, `#pragma`, `SuppressMessage`), licence, copyright and SPDX headers, generated-file banners, shebang and encoding lines. A request or plan that asks to "document" behaviour never licenses comments. That text goes to an external document: a change list, or an API reference through `documenting api`. The one exception is a why for a specific value or condition that the code cannot show. Never write it yourself. Propose it to the user with path, line and text. Only an approval recorded with `harness comment --path

--text ""` lets it past `guard.comments`, the hook that denies an edit adding a comment line. Example: `const ROUNDING = 0.5` rounds half-up because the tariff table is published that way. No name says that, so propose `src/fee.ts:42 "half-up: the tariff table is published that way"` and write it only after the user approves. If your change makes an existing comment stale, delete it; never reword it. Leave other existing comments as they are.

# Writing rules

Always loaded. They shape how text reads, never what work gets done; a verdict token or a template heading always wins over them.

No em dashes or en dashes anywhere, headings and lists included. Use a comma, a colon, parentheses, or two sentences; write "10 to 15" for a range. Hyphens stay inside compound words, identifiers, paths and flags.

Default to short paragraphs. Use a list only for enumerable items: files, options, ordered steps, a table of values. Explanation and reasoning are prose.

Plain English a B2 reader follows: "use" not "utilise", "fix" not "remediate". Keep the precise engineering term (idempotency, migration, bounded context) and add a one-line gloss when it may be unfamiliar. Give one concrete example with real values when you explain something.

Lead with the answer or the action. No preamble ("Let me", "Great question"), no closer ("Hope this helps"), no narration of tool use, no padded recap. Scale the reply to the ask.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.
